expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC

If you’re limited on space, don’t let the length of a rowing machine deter you. While there are many great rowing machines on the market, there are also some awesome compact alternatives that offer all the same tech features you’ll find in other cardio machines.

During our search for the best compact rowing machine, we found an array of excellent standalone options and options that fit in well with other top-rated home gym equipment. We considered the overall footprint and other key features, and scoured the reviews to see what users had to say about each product. Below is our list of the best compact home rowing machines available.

The rowing machines included in this list were carefully selected based on what most users would want out of a rowing machine, keeping in mind that they needed to have a smaller footprint and folding or upright storage options. We evaluated each choice based on size, portability, cost, high-tech features, versatility, and durability. We also scoured the reviews to see what users had to say about each rowing machine.

On the Hydrow website, the Hydrow Wave is rated 4.6/5 stars with over 9,000 reviews at the time of writing. It’s the brand’s compact, budget-friendly option for those who want to elevate their at-home workout routine. The length is just 80 inches, which is the shortest on this list, and the overall size is 30 percent shorter than the original Hydrow Rower. You cannot fold it, but there is the option to store it upright using The Hydrow Wave Vertical Anchor. This is a wall-mounted strap that holds the rower upright. It costs an additional $190, which is a bit on the pricey side.

The frame is made of aluminum and steel. It has a flat anthracite polymer body, which is a durable and lightweight material. The handle has an ergonomic design for a low-stress grip, and the strap is made from water- and rot-resistant polyester webbing. It also has a patented electromagnetic drag system that mimics the experience of rowing on open water.

Overall, the reviews on the Hydrow website are positive, and many mention how quiet the machine is and how much they like the small footprint. One review says, “The machine is such great quality. It’s quiet and sleek looking.” The critical reviews make up 3 percent of the overall reviews and state issues like non-working parts being delivered. However, Hydrow has responded to each review to resolve any issues.

The NordicTrack RW700 has a 10-inch HD touchscreen you can tilt and pivot to follow along with an iFIT workout led by your favorite trainer on or off the rower. An iFIT subscription is $39 per month, and you’ll have access to live and on-demand classes. Membership to the fitness app is not required to use the rower; however, you won’t have access to trainer-led classes without it.

A trainer-led rowing workout gives you the option to row on the open water for a more scenic experience, and there are also studio sessions. The resistance is adjusted automatically among 26 resistance levels during each class, so you don’t need to worry about stopping to make changes. The oversized foot pedals have adjustable nylon foot straps with quick release, which is excellent for those who want to incorporate movements off the rower into their workout.

The rail is 87 inches long and made from durable steel. It has an inertia-enhanced flywheel, so it should maintain a smooth rotation. If you have a shared space, the NordicTrack RW700 rower has a magnetic resistance system that creates tension against the flywheel without touching, making it a quieter option. After your workout, this magnetic rowing machine can be moved using the front wheels, but it can’t be folded.

The flywheel has been designed to maintain inertia and rotate smoothly, and the steel rail is oversized to help keep you stable. The large, pivoting foot pedals with adjustable nylon straps keep your feet in place, and the seat is molded with comfort in mind.

If you like to incorporate other movements into your rowing workout or train off of the rower, the Echelon Row-s has a 22-inch HD touchscreen that can be flipped 180 degrees. While an Echelon Fit subscription is not required, the extra $35/month workout app gives you access to over 40 live classes and more than 1,000 on-demand workouts from its library, including rowing, biking, running, and functional training classes.

The ergonomic design of the seat and the ability to adjust the foot platforms to a comfortable position help you maintain proper posture and alignment. If you’re short on space, the length goes from 84 inches long to just 41 inches long when folded. On the Echelon website, this rower is rated 4.6/5 stars. “The machine looks great, operates very quietly, and gives a great workout no matter your level,” says reviewer Brett P.

Dimensions: 87.02" L x 22.0" W x 47.24" H

Storage: Folds in half for vertical storage

Available programming: Live and on-demand workouts, scenic rows

The NordicTrack RW600 balances great tech features and an accessible price, making it a great value. The 10-inch screen is an excellent option for those who want to take instructor-led classes using an iFIT membership. NordicTrack’s patented Silent Magnetic Resistance can be adjusted up to 26 levels automatically in an iFIT class or manually as needed.

The pivoting foot pedals are oversized, and the nylon straps keep your feet secure. The handlebar has a soft grip, and the molded seat is designed to help you feel comfortable. When your workout is finished, the NordicTrack RW600 can be folded and stored out of the way.

What factors should you consider before you pull the trigger on a rower? Here’s what we’d recommend you take into account as you ponder your purchase decision:

Once you’ve decided on your rower location, it’s a good idea to measure the length, width, and height of your space to determine what size machine works best. You’ll want to measure height to see if you have enough clearance for rowers to be stored upright.

After measuring, think about how much you’re willing to spend. Take into consideration any additional costs such as a monthly subscription. Some rowers also have add-ons for purchase, such as a lumbar support system or seat upgrade.

Ask yourself: How many levels of resistance do I need? Am I looking for an HD touchscreen with trainer-led classes or do I prefer a more simplistic display? Other features such as a magnetic resistance system may be important if you’re in a shared space and need a quieter machine. The rower’s maximum height and/or weight capacity may also play a role in your decision as well.

Rowing allows you to implement low-impact, cardio-based training, and you can adjust the resistance for a strength-focused session. It’s a full-body workout that uses 86 percent of your muscles. With each stroke, you’re using your core and legs for the initial pull and finishing the rowing movement by using your upper body. Since you’re in a seated position, there’s less pressure on your knee and ankle joints.

Getting all four types of exercise (endurance, strength, balance, and flexibility) has benefits, according to The National Institute of Health (NIH). A rowing machine can be utilized for two types: endurance and strength. Many rowing machines have built-in programs or subscriptions that offer classes geared toward building strength and endurance.

Rowing is a great way to build strength and endurance while working various muscle groups. There are choices to suit a variety of budgets with different storage options and sizes. Figuring out how much space you have, your price range and the features you’d like will help you choose the best compact rowing machine for you.

The machines on this list range from just over $700 to around $2,000. You can find a rower in your price range, but if you opt for a rower under, say, $200, you may be compromising quality.

Typically, rowing machine length ranges between six to nine feet with more compact options at six or seven feet long.

The level of resistance that’s best for you depends on your fitness level, experience, and goals. Overall, you don’t want your workout to be too easy or so challenging you don’t accomplish the goal of your training session.

Compact rowing machines usually have air or magnetic resistance, and some options implement both.

#8818. Build Muscle Without Exercise? What Science Says About Using Creatine Without Lifting

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Creatine has been around the gym long enough to have survived several generations of invention. And reinvention. And re-re-invention… Let’s just say it’s been a supplement industry staple for decades; it’s cheap, well studied, and, when combined with resistance training, actually useful. Naturally, that wasn’t sexy enough. So, now the Internet has served up a study suggesting you can take creatine, skip the gym, and build muscle anyway. The next sound in my brain after I read it was Ronnie Coleman’s voice in my head sayin’ his famous line: “Everybody wants to be a bodybuilder, but nobody wants to lift no heavy-ass weights.”

But the study is real! Researchers at Texas A&M published it in August in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, and the results have been making the rounds again this fall. I’m very familiar with the ISSN, I’ve presented at one of its conventions. I know several of the members. The organization is legit. And Texas A&M is no joke either.

Researchers recruited 73 sedentary adults between the ages of 45 and 65 for the 12-week study. Of those, 64 completed it. Some chose to follow an exercise-and-diet program. Others didn’t. Within those groups, participants were randomly assigned either ten grams of creatine monohydrate a day or a placebo.

Then this happened. The non-exercisers taking creatine gained about 2.4 pounds of lean tissue on their body-composition scans. The non-exercisers taking a placebo didn’t show the same gain. The creatine group also improved on some strength tests. So, yes, something interesting happened. But is it what we’re afraid it is?

Notice I said “lean tissue,” not two and a half pounds of brand-new muscle. The researchers used DXA scans to measure body composition. Those scans are useful, but they don’t distinguish freshly built muscle protein from all the water sitting inside lean tissue. Creatine increases water stored in muscle, especially when people first start taking it. The study didn’t directly measure changes in body water, so nobody can tell you how much of that apparent gain was actual new muscle.

There’s another detail that tends to disappear somewhere between the scientific journal and the breathless headline. The no-exercise comparison involved just thirteen creatine users and thirteen placebo users. That’s not worthless. It’s also not the population of a medium-sized city. And the researchers randomized the supplement, not the decision to exercise. Participants chose whether to join the training program, so comparisons between exercisers and non-exercisers aren’t the same as a fully randomized test of exercise itself.

The people who did train combined resistance and aerobic exercise three times a week with a calorie-restricted diet. Creatine users in that group gained nearly three pounds of lean tissue and showed greater improvements in several performance measures. That’s interesting, too, although the study can’t tell us that creatine replaces lifting. If anything, the bigger picture still favors the traditional arrangement: take the supplement if you want, but keep showing up and doing the work.

The investigators also reported some promising changes in memory tests, blood lipids, and blood-sugar markers. I’m not dismissing those findings. But they tested a lot of outcomes in a relatively small study, and the authors themselves say the individual cognitive and metabolic results are exploratory. That’s scientist speak for “hmm… now do it again with more people.”

For completeness, the study was funded by a foundation gift. A creatine manufacturer supplied the supplements and paid for one laboratory assay, and the senior researcher disclosed a position on that company’s scientific advisory board. That doesn’t make the results false. It does make disclosure worth reading, which is something every person reporting supplement research ought to do before writing a headline.

None of this changes my opinion of creatine. It’s one of the few products on the shelf with a substantial body of evidence behind it. Ten grams daily was the dose in this experiment; it doesn’t suddenly replace the more familiar 3- to 5-gram maintenance approach used by many lifters. And if you have kidney disease or other medical issues, a conversation with your clinician would be appropriate.

So can creatine help somebody who doesn’t lift? Possibly. This trial suggests it might, and that’s worth investigating. Has anybody proved that a scoop of powder builds meaningful muscle while you sit on your ass? Not from these data. The supplement is interesting precisely because it may do more than we once thought. And what we once thought was pretty damn good. We don’t have to turn it into magic dust to appreciate that.

#8817. The Brooks Launch 12 Helps You Run Fast—and Save Big

This affordable trainer has racing shoe DNA.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

The Launch 12 is cushier than a racing flat but can handle hard workouts on the track and on the road. The affordable trainer—a bargain buy for $120—won’t break the bank, but it doesn’t feel cheaply made. The Launch has that Brooks touch; the comfy fit that securely locks your foot inside an airy mesh upper.

We included the Launch 12 in our Best Affordable Shoes guide because it’s an excellent choice for runners wanting a designated trainer for fast days. It’s also a sweet, cheaper lower-stacked alternative in a sea of towering, high-cushioned models.

For the runner who says the Brooks Ghost is too bulky and boxy, the Launch 12 could be your sole mate.

I’ve added track workouts to my training this year after finally overcoming my fear of the dreaded all-eyes-on-me oval. It’s fun to go balls-to-the-wall in today’s super trainers and high stacks during speed sessions, but I sometimes desire a more grounded, minimally designed trainer to really test my fitness. The Brooks Launch 12 is that shoe.

Finding out there’s DNA Flash v2 foam in the Launch 12 is like finding an Easter egg in a movie. It’s a callout to the Hyperion Elite 4, Brooks’s premium racing shoe model. The shoe originally had nitrogen-infused DNA Flash v2 foam to pump up your ride before switching to DNA Gold (PEBA, baby) in the Hyperion Elite 5. But it can’t be ignored that DNA Flash v2 was a form of Brooks’s original super foam.

This gives the shoe a firm, snappy ride with plenty of padding for shock absorption. It’s not max-cushioned, and certainly not super trainer height at 35 mm, but it packs plenty of support for hard and long efforts.

“Typically, I’m a fan of the middle ground when it comes to trainers,” said Content Hyper Editor Ashley Tysiac. “I like to have a shoe with enough cushioning that I feel like my feet are supported, but not too much that I feel like my feet are being weighed down by bricks. This shoe was a pleasant break from some of the heavier, maximalist trainers that I’ve tried in the past couple of years. It’s a lightweight shoe that provides a firm ride.

“There’s not a ton of give to the shoe or spring in its step, but I didn’t mind that. The firm, easy ride was something I could enjoy on regular runs, long runs, and even some runs with faster-paced segments in the middle.”

The Launch 12 is built like a track shoe with its narrow, streamlined last. Tester Ricky Snyder said he had no issues with the fit, saying everything was “perfect, no hot spots or cramping in the toe box, no hard or rubbing plastic parts.”

However, Tysiac—and I—found the Launch 12’s midfoot a wee too snug.

“I wasn’t a huge fan of the lacing system,” she said. “No matter how many times I loosened and re-laced my shoes, it always felt too tight through the midfoot area, causing some noticeable discomfort.”

As a runner with wide feet, I couldn’t agree more with Tysiac. Compared to Brooks’s Hyperion 3, which also has DNA Flash v2 foam along a knit upper that hugs your foot, I felt the Launch 12 was much narrower and constrictive. The Hyperion 3 costs $20 extra, and speaking from experience, it could be worth the spending if you have wide feet like mine.

The Launch 12 is a shoe for runners looking to find a cheaper alternative to the more costly speedwork ones on the market, but it’s also for runners who miss shoes pre-super foam. The shoe may have an older midsole version of Brooks’s special sauce, but the ride takes you back to simple days, when a firmly cushioned trainer was all you needed to get in a run.

“I took out the Brooks Launch 12 on a variety of runs, including regular runs, regular runs with pickups in the middle, and long runs. Perhaps the shoe’s best feature that stands out is how light it is, providing a ride that doesn’t feel too bogged down. They felt light enough to rip off some faster-paced fartlek segments during the middle of a regular run, but still supportive enough to make it through a longer run.”

For $120, you’ll find a trainer that can take on multiple workouts. The Launch 12 is a good deal for the runner looking to save.

#8816. ZOLTÁN BÁTHORY OF FIVE FINGER DEATH PUNCH IS COMMITTED TO HIS MUSIC, COMMUNITIES, AND JUDO

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

The members of Five Finger Death Punch have been busy lately. Their 10th studio album, Legacy, was recently released, and they began their 20th Anniversary World Tour in July with the North American leg. Zoltán Báthory is the founder of 5FDP as well as their rhythm guitarist and primary songwriter. When asked his thoughts about celebrating two decades of success, Báthory was proud but more grateful for their legions of fans.

“It was always the people’s band,” he said with a smile. The Las Vegas band has been around so long, they were first getting attention on MySpace. Báthory recalled experts writing in magazines that they wouldn’t be around very long, but staying true to themselves and focusing only on the music has been their key to success.

“We just kept pushing and the people stayed with us.”

Báthory knows their music is not for everybody, but he hears stories all the time from people who have told them that hits such as “Under and Over It” and “Wash it All Away” are on their workout playlists or may have helped them get past a hard time in their lives. Báthory views that as a badge of honor because he himself trains in Flex Lewis’ Dragon Lair gym in Las Vegas and is as much a part of that community as he is the hard rock and heavy metal space.

“I’m proud of that because these are my people.”

5FDP also has a large following in the military and first responder communities. Aside from their many hits, they are known for their support of veterans and firefighters through donations to the Call of Duty Endowment fund, doing other fundraisers through their music, and Báthory has served on boards for groups like the Home Deployment Project.

“When I get a military guy telling me, ‘It’s difficult to be in a war zone. But I got up every day and listened to you guys, and it not just got me ready for the day, it got me through the day.’ That kind of gives us a justification that we’re doing something good. So, it also keeps us going. I love it.”

Báthory’s love for music and working out may only be rivaled by his passion for judo. Growing up in Hungary, judo in his home country was more popular than it is in North America. He first started following the discipline at age 9 and was entering tournaments before becoming a teenager. Báthory felt that taking up judo has done far more for him than improving his skills alone.

“I can say and I can claim that that philosophy of judo was one of the key elements of me becoming successful,” he explained. “It rewires your mind, and you start to think very differently.”

Báthory still makes time to train and actively competes in tournaments to this day. He has also taken up jiujitsu and reports having black belts in both disciplines. But he is not only trying to be better in martial arts but for it as well. Judo is an Olympic sport, and athletes internationally are very committed to excelling in it. The American judo scene is not as prominent as it is in other countries, but Báthory is trying to change that and wants to help those Americans looking to compete in the 2028 Summer Olympic Games in Los Angeles, California.

“I’ve worked with USA Judo and IJF (International Judo Federation). It’s one of my missions to make judo more visible in America, for more people to practice it.”

Báthory’s passion and commitment to his mission is more than moral support and advocacy. He has even made a financial commitment to this goal.

“I want the American team to do really well in judo. I’m even financially supporting the judo team. A portion of the tickets of this tour is actually going to USA Judo so they can afford the participation in training camps.”

Even though they have two decades behind them, 5FDP is as popular as ever, and tickets to their shows have already been selling fast. Like any elite band, they have had their shares of growing pains and critics, but the loyal fanbase and joy they get from creating music and performing it continues to fuel their desire.

Báthory has as much love and appreciation for their supporters as they do for the band. That’s because of the communities those fans are in; military, first responders, athletes, martial arts, and others who are looking for something positive to lean on. Báthory proclaimed that 5FDP will continue to make music and do their best to support their fans not only because they support them but because of what they do.

“What is the common denominator between these people? They all help other people.”

You can learn more about 5FDP, their tour, and Legacy by going to their website and subscribing to their YouTube channel.

Follow Báthory on Instagram @zoltanbathory and @zoltanbjj.

#8815. The Best Protein Powders for Weight Loss, According to a Certified Nutrition Coach

Protein powder can help you maintain muscle mass while eating in a calorie deficit. We tested more than 100 protein powders and found nine we think are best for weight loss.

Written by Stephen Sheehan, CPT × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC Last updated on Feb 19, 2025

expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC

When someone says they want to lose weight, what they really mean is they want to shed excess body fat. However, without a well-designed plan in place, a calorie deficit leads you to lose both fat and valuable muscle tissue. To minimize muscle loss, it’s crucial to incorporate resistance training, quality sleep, and a high-protein diet into your regular routine.

Protein plays a multifaceted role in weight management, influencing factors like hunger levels, metabolism, and muscle preservation. While heavy resistance training provides the necessary stimulus, signaling to the body that existing muscle should be retained, a high-protein diet ensures the body has an ample supply of amino acids. This prevents your body from metabolizing muscle tissue for energy.

The best protein powders provide a convenient and lean source of the muscle-building macronutrient, helping you hit your daily protein goals while also maintaining a calorie deficit. We tested more than 100 protein powders and selected nine products we think are best for weight loss.

This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any new supplement or exercise regimen.

We chose these products based on a number of factors, including:

I chose Transparent Labs as the best protein powder for weight loss because it has a very high ratio of protein to the total number of calories: 28 grams to 130 calories. This helps you maximize protein consumption during a caloric deficit, which helps prevent you from losing muscle while you’re losing weight. It’s also third-party tested, Informed Choice certified, and completely artificial ingredient-free. And it comes in 15 flavor options.

I’ve tried a number of different flavors from Transparent Labs and Chocolate Peanut Butter is by far my favorite, followed closely by Mocha. I found they mixed easily in both a blender and a conventional shaker bottle. Whenever I’m trying to cut weight, I find this delicious protein powder helps curb my sweet tooth and tide me over between meals.

While I didn’t personally experience this, some customer reviews mention it can be challenging to get in contact with Transparent Labs’ customer service team.

Jacked Factory Authentic Iso has 25 grams of protein per serving, 2 grams of carbohydrates, and just 0.5 grams of fat, which is the least amount of fat of any powder on our list. If you’re looking to lose weight, this macronutrient profile will help keep you on the right track. However, something to keep in mind: This protein powder is sweetened with sucralose, which is an artificial sweetener—studies link these sweeteners to increased cancer risk. Additionally, unlike most brands on our list, Jacked Factory doesn’t do third-party testing on its products. This means there isn’t a guarantee the ingredients are pure and match the ingredient label.

Kessler tried Jacked Factory Authentic Iso and was impressed. “This is the only protein powder I’ve tried that didn’t settle at all,” he says. “I found it a bit too sweet, but if you’re looking for a powder that tastes like dessert, you should opt for this one.”

If you’re looking for one of the best vegan protein powders that also works with a weight loss diet, Ka’Chava is a great choice. This vegan protein powder is marketed as a “whole-body meal,” which means it’s designed as a meal replacement rather than an addition to a meal or snack, like the other protein powders on our list. That’s why the calorie, carbohydrate, and fat counts (240, 25 grams, and 7 grams, respectively), are higher. The carb count is high for those on a low-carb diet, so that’s something to look out for. However, it packs in 25 grams of plant protein, derived from a combination of peas, brown rice, and quinoa, which will help preserve muscle while on a weight loss diet.

Tester Zoe Ettinger, a C.N.C.-in-training, uses this protein powder often. “I’m a big fan of Ka’Chava. It tastes delicious mixed in a smoothie with some frozen blueberries,” she says. “I also like that it also has adaptogens, probiotics, greens, and probiotics. I notice a difference in how good I feel when I take Ka’Chava regularly,” she says.

One thing to note about Ka’Chava is that it is the most expensive option on our list at $79.99 for a 15-serving bag. While the price reflects the fact that this protein powder is intended as a meal replacement, it’s still a big investment.

I chose Nutricost as the best protein powder for weight loss available on Amazon because its calorie and macronutrient profile is ideal for shedding pounds. Nutricost has a high protein content per serving, which is important for weight loss as protein can help enhance satiety and preserve muscle mass while in a deficit. With minimal fat and carbohydrates, this protein ensures you get the maximum protein intake without the added calories, making it an ideal choice for those looking to lose weight efficiently.

The taste and mixability of this protein are also top-notch. I tested the Vanilla flavor; it blended excellently in both milk and water and had an authentic vanilla taste profile. Despite using artificial sweeteners, which often make products sickly sweet, I found the sweetness level to be on point. However, if you’re trying to avoid artificial sweeteners, choose Promix or Transparent Labs, which use natural sweeteners.

Huel is our favorite meal replacement for weight loss because it has a great protein-to-carb ratio. Huel has 40 grams of protein per serving, the most of any protein powder on our list, and 24 grams of carbs. While this might be more carbs than ideal for those on a keto diet, it’s a solid portion for most. Carbs are an essential nutrient and according to experts, you can consume 100 to 150 grams a day and still lose weight.

Kessler tried Huel in Chocolate and Vanilla. “The Chocolate flavor was great, probably because it uses real cocoa powder, which gave it an authentic chocolate flavor,” he says. “The Vanilla wasn’t as good—it didn’t really taste like vanilla and had an artificial aftertaste.” He notes that it doesn’t mix very well, but says it made him feel great. “Other similar products, like Transparent Labs Mass Gainer, give me an upset stomach. But I felt great after taking Huel Black Edition,” he says.

Promix is our favorite clean protein powder because it’s third-party tested and results are easily viewable on Promix’s website. Those results show this product is tested for heavy metals and verified gluten-free. And beyond these positive results, this protein powder has one of the most simple formulas on our list. Vanilla, for example, has just four ingredients, and Promix doesn’t use any artificial ingredients.

This protein powder, like others on our list, has a solid protein-to-carb ratio for weight loss (25 grams to 7 grams, respectively). A 2020 study found consuming a higher portion of protein versus carbs helped participants lose weight and prevented them from gaining the weight back.

I tried the Vanilla flavor of this protein powder. I enjoyed it for the most part, but it wasn’t quite sweet enough for my taste. And I wish it mixed a little better—there were some clumps after mixing.

One thing to note about Promix is that while it has been third-party tested, it hasn’t been third-party tested for sport specifically. This means it hasn’t been tested for substances banned in athletic competitions. So if you’re an athlete planning to compete, opt for a powder that’s Informed Sport Certified or NSF Certified for Sport.

One of my favorite casein protein powders is Casein+ from Legion Athletics. I chose Casein+ because it’s all-natural, meaning it’s free from artificial sweeteners, flavors, and colors, and it’s third-party tested by Labdoor for purity and potency. This product provides 25 grams of protein per serving and only contains 110 calories, regardless of the flavor you choose. This protein-to-calorie ratio is ideal for weight loss.

Along with whey, casein is a type of protein found in milk and is characterized by its slow digestion and absorption. This prolonged digestion makes it an ideal option for people looking to manage hunger levels and maintain a consistent supply of amino acids over an extended timeframe—such as during sleep or when going a long time between meals. By providing a steady stream of protein to the muscles, casein helps mitigate the risk of muscle breakdown that often accompanies calorie restriction. As a result, incorporating a casein protein powder into your diet can be a strategic move to help support your weight loss goals.

Tester Brandon Lunsford, C.P.T., tried the Dutch Chocolate flavor, saying it reminded him of a dark chocolate bar that isn’t too rich or too sweet. The only downside is that casein protein has a different consistency than whey. It’s generally thicker and often takes longer to dissolve. Lunsford noticed this during his testing, saying the product had a “slightly chalky aftertaste.”

Naked Whey’s Unflavored protein stands out for its simplicity and purity; its single-ingredient formula consists of whey protein concentrate sourced for grass-fed cows. This simplicity aligns with the brand’s commitment to transparency, priding itself on avoiding additives, fillers, or artificial ingredients in its products.

With its neutral taste profile, this protein powder is very versatile, letting you integrate the protein powder seamlessly into your favorite recipes or smoothies without altering the flavor profile. Kessler tried the Unflavored version and says it “has a very slight vanilla taste to it.” He also detected a note of earthiness, but says “It would be really good mixed into a smoothie.” However, he mentions the two-scoop serving size can feel like a lot, so he recommends using extra liquid when blending it.

If you’re someone who prefers a flavored protein powder, you’ll be happy to know Naked also offers five flavored options, including Chocolate, Vanilla, Strawberry, Chocolate Peanut Butter, and Double Chocolate. Naked only uses coconut sugar to sweeten its protein supplements, which isn’t nearly as sweet as artificial sweeteners like sucralose or acesulfame potassium.

We chose Sports Research as our best protein powder for weight loss and muscle gain because it has a solid protein-to-calorie ratio (25 grams to 140 calories), is Informed Sport Certified, is fairly priced at $1.20 per serving, and tastes great, according to testers.

From a nutritional standpoint, Sports Research stacks up well against many of its competitors. The per-serving content for protein (25 grams), calories (140), and carbs (2 grams) compares favorably with most of the choices on our list, although the fat per serving (3.5 grams for Vanilla and 4 grams for Dutch Chocolate) is on the high side. Other ingredients include vitamin D, which has been linked to muscle health in recent research.

Tester Cory Kessler, C.N.C., C.P.T., tried the Creamy Vanilla flavor. “When I mixed it with milk it almost tasted like vanilla ice cream,” he says. “But when I mixed it with water it diluted the flavor, and all I could taste was the sweetness,” he warns. He also notes that it mixed very well, and “wasn’t gritty or clumpy at all.”

Whether from powder or whole food sources, protein aids weight loss mainly by:

Protein powder can be an effective tool in helping you achieve your weight loss goals. Drinking a protein powder shake or smoothie provides a quick, easy way to consume high amounts of protein with a limited amount of calories, fat, and carbohydrates. One of the main benefits of protein powder is that it’s often extremely lean, with a very high ratio of protein to total number of calories. This makes protein powder an efficient way to hit your daily protein target while adhering to your calorie guidelines.

Choose a protein powder with a significant amount of protein, typically around 25 grams per serving. If you have weight loss goals, a whey, soy, or pea protein isolate is likely your best bet since they are ultra-filtered to remove excess carbohydrates and fats.

When you have weight loss goals, it’s best to choose a protein powder with a moderate calorie count per serving, e.g., 100 to 160 calories. You should also ensure the majority of those calories come from protein, as this will best support your weight loss progress. Remember, protein is four calories per gram, so you can expect a supplement that has 25 grams of protein to have around 110 to 120 calories if it’s extremely lean.

It’s important to check the ingredients list of the supplement to ensure the product is free from added sugars or unnecessary fillers. Although these ingredients may contribute to the flavor, sweetness, and creaminess of the supplement, they often come with added calories. It’s generally best to select protein powders with minimal ingredients.

Occasionally, protein powders contain ingredients such as creatine, probiotics, or branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs). While these aren’t necessary, it’s important to assess whether these added ingredients align with your health and fitness goals, and whether it’s worth choosing a protein powder that offers these options.

Regardless of your goals, choose a protein powder with a flavor and consistency you enjoy. I know this seems obvious, but if you dislike the taste, then you’re far less likely to use the protein powder on a consistent basis, if at all.

As a certified nutrition coach, I advise my clients to choose a protein powder that’s been third-party tested for quality, purity, and safety, especially when I’m working with athletes. This ensures your supplement is free from contaminants, including banned substances, and is deemed safe for consumption. Third-party testing also holds supplement companies accountable, providing assurance that the ingredients in the product align with the information provided on the supplement facts label.

Whenever you’re purchasing a dietary supplement, you should look for one that aligns with your specific health and fitness goals. With weight loss in mind, it’s typically recommended to avoid products with added sugars, or excessive amounts of carbohydrates and fats. Some consumers may also choose to avoid products with artificial additives, such as sweeteners, flavors, and colors, which are routinely found in protein powder supplements. If you’re looking for an all-natural protein powder with minimal ingredients, consider Transparent Labs 100% Grass-Fed Whey or protein powders from Naked Nutrition.

As a certified nutrition coach, I think it’s important to emphasize that a protein powder isn’t a necessity for weight loss success. However, due to its convenience and effectiveness, it does offer some notable benefits when used as part of a holistic approach to weight loss that includes resistance training, quality sleep, and healthy lifestyle habits. Consuming a high-protein diet, especially during a weight-loss phase, helps manage hunger levels and improves muscle preservation. If a protein powder can help you hit your daily protein targets while still maintaining a calorie deficit, then I think it’s worth incorporating into your regular routine.

Protein shakes are an excellent way to help preserve lean muscle mass when pursuing your weight loss goals. If weight loss is your primary objective, I’d suggest opting for a whey protein isolate, such as Transparent Labs 100% Grass-Fed Whey. This protein powder is incredibly lean, meaning the majority of calories come from protein alone. This can help you achieve your daily protein targets without over-consuming calories from the additional carbohydrates and fats commonly found in a whey protein concentrate.

Weight loss strategies vary from person to person, however, individuals with weight loss goals should aim for at least 1.2 to 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight. (This equates to approximately 0.5 to 0.7 grams of protein per pound of body weight.) This range should provide enough protein to support muscle mass while maintaining a calorie deficit, which is necessary for weight loss.

With protein powder for weight loss, certain protein sources are considered “leaner” than others. For example, whey protein isolates benefit from various kinds of processing and filtration that lower the fat and carbohydrates in the finished product. The main drawback with some plant-based proteins is that they can be naturally higher in carbs. Fortunately, high-quality plant protein powders could deliver comparable results to whey protein in terms of promoting lean body mass.Lean animal proteins include chicken breast, fish, and eggs. Even certain cuts of beef (sirloin) and pork (loin) are considered lean. Greek yogurt, tofu, beans, and lentils are among the non-animal sources of lean protein.

When focusing on weight loss, it’s best to steer clear of calorie-rich beverages such as sugary sodas and sports drinks, fruit juices, and alcohol. Instead, choose options like water, seltzer, black coffee, and unsweetened tea, all of which are essentially calorie-free. Avoiding calorie-dense beverages allows you to allocate those calories to food instead, which should help improve your satiety or feelings of fullness after meals.

There’s no protein that targets belly fat loss specifically. However, prioritizing lean protein, such as a whey protein isolate, can be beneficial for your overall weight loss goals. Whey protein isolates are processed to minimize the carbohydrate and fat content, maximizing the protein-to-calorie ratio of the supplement. This makes them an efficient option to support your intake of dietary protein while maintaining a calorie deficit.

#8814. What Is a Timeshare? Why Financial Experts Say Avoid Them

A timeshare is a shared ownership or usage right in a vacation property. You pay an upfront purchase price — typically $20,000 to $40,000 — plus annual maintenance fees that currently average $1,120 per year and increase 3-5% annually. In exchange, you get the right to use a resort unit for a specific period each year, usually one week.

The timeshare industry generates over $10 billion in annual sales, and roughly 9.9 million U.S. households own at least one timeshare. But ownership satisfaction varies dramatically, and the financial reality rarely matches the sales presentation delivered during high-pressure resort tours.

Deeded (Fixed Week): You own a fractional interest in a specific unit during a specific week each year. This is actual real property — you receive a deed, it's recorded with the county, and you can theoretically sell, rent, or bequeath it. The problem: the secondary market for these deeds values most of them at near zero.

Right-to-Use (Leased): You purchase the right to use a property for a set number of years (typically 20-40 years) but don't own real estate. At the end of the term, your usage right expires with nothing to show for it. This is common with newer resort brands.

Points-Based Systems: Instead of a fixed week at a fixed resort, you purchase an annual allotment of points that can be redeemed at various properties within a resort network. Flexibility is the selling point, but availability at popular destinations during peak seasons is often limited — and points can inflate over time, requiring more points for the same week.

Timeshare companies spend an average of $4,000 in marketing costs per sale — and much of that goes toward the high-pressure sales presentations that are a signature of the industry. These presentations use urgency tactics ("this price is only available today"), comparison anchoring (showing the cost per vacation day), and emotional triggers ("don't you want the best for your family?"). The FI community's rule: never make a five-figure financial decision on the same day you learn about it. Walk away, run the numbers at home, and compare alternatives. The offer will still be available tomorrow — despite what the salesperson claims.

Timeshare sales presentations focus on the purchase price and the "cost per vacation night." What they don't emphasize is the total lifetime cost, which includes mandatory annual fees that increase every year, special assessments for major repairs, exchange fees if you want to trade your week, and the opportunity cost of that capital.

Let's run the real numbers on a typical timeshare over 20 years:

At $4,204 per week over 20 years — without accounting for the opportunity cost of the capital — you can book luxury vacation rentals in most destinations for less money with zero long-term commitment.

This is the most important financial fact about timeshares: they have almost no resale value. The American Resort Development Association (ARDA) — the timeshare industry's own trade group — acknowledges that resale prices are a fraction of the original purchase price. In practice, most timeshares on the secondary market are listed for $1 or even offered for free, because the buyer inherits the mandatory annual maintenance fees.

Websites like RedWeek, TUG (Timeshare Users Group), and eBay are filled with timeshare listings at $0-$1. Owners often can't give them away because the ongoing fee obligation makes them a liability, not an asset. This is the fundamental difference between a timeshare and a real investment: real investments appreciate or generate income. Timeshares depreciate to zero and generate mandatory ongoing costs.

If you already own a timeshare and want out, here are your realistic options:

Rescission Period: Most states give you 3-15 days after purchase to cancel without penalty. This is your best exit — if you're within this window, cancel immediately in writing via certified mail.

Sell on the Resale Market: List on TUG (Timeshare Users Group), RedWeek, or eBay. Set your expectations: you'll likely sell for $0-$1, and the "sale" is really about transferring the maintenance fee obligation to a willing buyer.

Contact the Resort's Deed-Back Program: Some major resort chains (Wyndham, Marriott, Hilton) offer deed-back or surrender programs where you can return the timeshare to the resort. Eligibility varies and there may be fees, but this is a legitimate exit path.

Timeshare Exit Companies: Proceed with Extreme Caution. The timeshare exit industry is plagued with scams. Legitimate exit attorneys exist, but many "exit companies" charge $3,000-$10,000 upfront and deliver nothing. The FTC and state attorneys general have pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Before hiring anyone, check their BBB rating, look for complaints with your state attorney general, and never pay the full fee upfront.

The FI community has consistently found that travel rewards credit cards, vacation rental platforms, and strategic booking provide better vacation value than timeshare ownership:

Here's the number that should end the timeshare debate for any FI-focused person: the average timeshare's annual maintenance fee ($1,120) invested in index funds at a 10% average return grows to $72,000+ in 20 years and $203,000+ in 30 years. Add the opportunity cost of the $24,140 purchase price invested instead, and the 30-year FI impact exceeds $440,000. That's nearly half a million dollars diverted from your FI number for one week of vacation per year at a resort you didn't choose.

Travel well, spend less, keep your FI timeline intact.

Choose a card that matches your spending patterns and offers flexible points or transferable miles. Sign-up bonuses alone often cover 1-2 free flights or hotel stays in the first year.

Pro tip: Pay the balance in full every month. Travel rewards only work financially if you never carry a balance and pay interest.

Instead of paying $1,120/year in mandatory timeshare fees, deposit that same amount monthly ($93/month) into a high-yield savings account earmarked for travel. You'll have $1,120+ per year to spend on any vacation, anywhere.

Research destinations on Airbnb, VRBO, and Booking.com. Booking 3-6 months ahead gets the best selection. Compare total costs including cleaning fees and service charges to timeshare equivalent costs.

Shifting your vacation by 2-4 weeks outside peak season saves 30-50% on flights and accommodation. Shoulder season often has better weather than peak season with fewer crowds.

If you were considering a $24,000 timeshare purchase, invest that money instead. At 10% average returns, $24,000 grows to $62,000 in 10 years and $161,000 in 20 years — all while you vacation on your own terms.

Pro tip: Set up automatic monthly investments for the amount you would have spent on timeshare financing payments.

A timeshare's purchase price ($24,140) plus 30 years of maintenance fees ($1,120/year growing at 3.5%) totals over $83,000 in direct costs. Invested in index funds at 10% average returns instead, that same money grows to over $440,000. That's the true cost of a timeshare — not the sticker price, but nearly half a million dollars of lost wealth-building potential over a career.

No. A timeshare is a prepaid vacation plan, not an investment. Timeshares depreciate to near-zero resale value, generate mandatory ongoing costs that increase annually, and cannot produce income for the owner in most cases. The timeshare industry itself has moved away from calling them investments because of regulatory scrutiny.

The average annual maintenance fee is $1,120, according to ARDA (the industry trade group). Fees increase an average of 3-5% per year and are mandatory — you must pay them whether or not you use your timeshare. Some resort areas (Hawaii, ski towns) charge $1,500-$2,500+ per year. Special assessments for major repairs can add $1,000-$5,000 in any given year.

Technically yes, but practically it's very difficult. The secondary market is flooded with inventory at $0-$1 prices because most owners are trying to escape their maintenance fee obligations. Resale companies that promise to sell your timeshare for thousands of dollars are almost always scams. The most realistic options are deed-back to the resort, transfer to a willing buyer at $0-$1, or working with a licensed timeshare exit attorney.

The resort will send your account to collections, report the delinquency to credit bureaus (damaging your credit score), and potentially pursue legal action. For deeded timeshares, the resort can foreclose on the property. Maintenance fee obligations are contractual and legally enforceable — you cannot simply walk away without consequences.

Some are, many are not. The FTC has pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Red flags include: demanding full payment ($3,000-$10,000) upfront, guaranteeing results, using high-pressure sales tactics similar to timeshare presentations, and lack of BBB accreditation. If you need exit help, consult a licensed real estate attorney in the state where the timeshare is located.

In very narrow circumstances: if you genuinely vacation at the same resort every year, the annual cost (maintenance fees amortized with purchase price) is lower than booking that same unit independently, and you purchased on the resale market for $0-$1 (avoiding the $24,000+ retail markup). Even then, you're locked into one destination with escalating fees. For most people, the flexibility and cost advantage of alternatives makes timeshares a poor choice.

A timeshare is a prepaid vacation plan with a near-zero resale value, mandatory escalating fees, and an extremely difficult exit process. The average timeshare costs over $84,000 across 20 years of ownership — and that money invested instead could grow to over $440,000 in 30 years. Modern alternatives like travel rewards cards, vacation rentals, and strategic off-peak booking deliver comparable or better vacation experiences with zero long-term commitment. If you're building toward financial independence, a timeshare is one of the most damaging financial products you can buy. If you already own one, explore deed-back programs or resale as your fastest path out.

#8813. The 5 Best Outdoor Saunas for Getting Your Sweat On in 2025

Experts explain how hot and cold wellness therapies could improve health. These outdoor saunas help you get these potential benefits at home.

Written by Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Stephen Sheehan, CPT Last updated on Mar 4, 2025

Sauna bathing is an age-old Nordic tradition that can have huge benefits for your overall wellness.

There are a variety of sauna styles available, from the traditional barrels to more modern cube designs with electric heaters, infrared heaters, or wood-burning stoves. Some newer models have high-tech features like surround-sound speakers, added LED light therapy, and charging docks for your electronics. However, all you need to reap the potential benefits of your sauna experience is a high-quality product you’ll actually use.

We found six of the best outdoor saunas and included a comprehensive guide for picking the right sauna for you. We also tapped Saloni Sharma, M.D., Medhat Mikhael, M.D., and Earric Lee, a postdoctoral researcher studying exercise science and Sport and Health Sciences faculty member at the University of Jyväskylä, Finland (a.k.a., sauna central), to help us understand how sauna use can benefit athletes during training.

This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any new supplement or exercise regimen.

If you’re seeking a more technology-forward sauna experience, Sun Home’s Luminar outdoor infrared sauna is an excellent model to invest in. This five-person model uses an infrared heating system, which you can control through your phone via a mobile app. Indoor saunas often have infrared heat, but Sun Home claims its Luminar model is more than 12.5 times more powerful at 500 watts than competitors. This sauna includes Bluetooth speakers and soothing LED chromotherapy, making sitting in a hot room more enticing to beginner bathers. Yes, it’s a pricey model, but it has ample features and floor-to-ceiling windows for a panoramic view of the outdoors.

According to SweatTent, you can set up the SweatTent Outdoor Sauna in about three minutes. It is somewhat portable because it is simple to put up and take down. The material is durable, insulated, and weather-proof, so you can leave the sauna outdoors indefinitely.

A wood-fired stove heats the SweatTent and comes with 20 pounds of sauna rocks, a fire poker, and heat-resistant gloves to feed the fire safely. The SweatTent is our favorite option for a complete sauna kit. It’s easy to set up, comparatively inexpensive, portable, and works well.

The Sun Home Luminar Sauna is a cube sauna with a carbonized wood exterior and dura-glass windows built to withstand any climate conditions. Luminar has a compact footprint compared to other two-person cube saunas. It uses a combination of infrared and full-spectrum heaters positioned to maintain optimum heat regardless of exterior conditions.

The choice of grade-A carbonized red cedar wood and thick double-pane glass throughout the sauna ensures durability and insulation. With nine heaters, including three far-infrared heaters under the bench and six full-spectrum heaters surrounding the cabin, the Luminar Outdoor Sauna guarantees an efficient and effective sauna session. Sun Home places these heaters strategically to envelop the users in 3D healing wavelengths from all angles.

You can control the Luminar temperature from an app to start heating your sauna before you get home. It has Bluetooth surround-sound speakers and a panoramic view through the dura-glass windows.

The Redwood Outdoors Barrel Sauna is a traditional barrel sauna made with Thermowood. It has all the features you need with nothing extra. We appreciate that you can customize several parts of this dry sauna, from the heating mechanism (you can go the Finnish sauna route with a Harvia electric heater or a wood-burning stove) to add-ons like a weather-resistant shingled roof and even a cold plunge tub. It has a spa-like sauna scent and dry heat, and comfortably fits four to six people.

One benefit of a Thermowood sauna is its durability and resistance to the elements. Redwood Outdoors says that, when properly cared for, this sauna should have an outdoor lifespan of 20 years.

The Redwood Outdoors Thermowood Cabin Sauna is our best outdoor sauna for cold climates because of its robust, weather-resistant construction. This sauna has a traditional Scandinavian design with Scandinavian softwood treated with intense heat to provide exceptional insulation. This design enhances its longevity and contributes to its energy efficiency, ensuring even heat distribution throughout the interior.

The Thermowood Cabin Sauna package includes a Harvia electric heater, wooden heater guard, water bucket and ladle, sauna rocks, and interior seating benches, providing all the necessary components for an authentic sauna experience.

If you’ve spent quality time in the locker room sauna, you’re committed to the wellness practice, and you live somewhere with outdoor space, a sauna might be an excellent investment for your health. “Researchers have found several possible health benefits from sauna use; most importantly, they have shown to help cardiovascular diseases—particularly high blood pressure and heart diseases—as well as acute and chronic pain and neurological diseases,” Mikhael says.

Putting a sauna inside can create some logistical challenges, though, from installation to insulation and more. An outdoor sauna might be easier to install, and it gets you closer to nature, as many of them have spacious windows. “One big bonus of outdoor saunas specifically is they exist outdoors,” Sharma says. “There is a problem in our society labeled Nature Deficit Disorder, which means we aren’t spending enough time outside. There are many proven benefits of being outdoors, and these saunas allow you to combine them with the potential benefits of heat therapy.”

Depending on your model, once your outdoor sauna is installed and ready to go, you can set the temperature via a manual dial, Bluetooth-enabled app, or touchscreen. The heat comes from sauna heaters or wood-burning stoves. Some outdoor saunas allow you to set the timer up to 36 hours in advance. From there, all you need to do is open the door, climb in, and relax.

As for timing, “Two to three 15- to 25-minute sessions per week are ideal,” says Mikhael. “After 15 to 25 minutes, people can benefit the most without feeling like they’re getting dehydrated or dizzy.”

Bring a book, crank up your music, or bring a friend to sweat it out with you—and remember to stay hydrated.

“You want to ensure you’re hydrated before and after,” says Sharma. “A sauna induces a lot of sweating, so you can get dehydrated very easily.” We recommend an electrolyte powder after use if you sweat a lot.

Ideally, you should be heading to your sauna soon as part of your post-workout routine, Lee says. “We found not only is a combination of exercise and sauna bathing stronger in its effects, but many cardiovascular benefits, like lower blood pressure, were sustained for a longer period afterward.”

Most saunas use electricity to run the lights and heaters. Low-tech wood stove-heated saunas might not need any power if there are no lights. There are some solar-powered saunas, too, if you want less strain on the environment (and your electric bill). You’ll just need to make sure you have a battery as a backup.

Given their size and weight, saunas are not very portable. So we’d recommend buying an outdoor sauna once you’re living in a permanent residence rather than an apartment or rental. But even then, life happens, and sometimes you need to move. You can move a constructed outdoor sauna, but it would likely need professional equipment to hoist it into a truck bed. There are very portable tent saunas—much more affordable than the outdoor ones on our list.

The outdoor saunas we recommend cost between $1,599 and $9,799. Based on our research, the lower end of the spectrum offers plenty of heat but fewer bells and whistles. The more pricey saunas can typically seat more people, have more temperature adjustments, provide more comfortable accommodations, and are made with higher-quality materials.

Many outdoor saunas on this list offer additional accessories a la carte. While these aren’t integral to your new sauna routine, they might make it more fun, luxe, and/or comfortable. Some standard accessories we noticed are outdoor showers, cold plunge tubs such as the Plunge, and wooden recliners. Nothing’s stopping you from DIY-ing those accessories, though.

Many wellness fads are short-lived trends (and even potentially harmful). But saunas have been staples in Scandinavian life for centuries, showing significant promise in improving your well-being. Our experts say regular sauna use can improve muscle soreness and even chronic pain.

If you’ve dabbled in heat therapy in the past and want to make it more of a long-term lifestyle (and you have the budget to match), an outdoor sauna can be a valuable and beneficial tool. But, like any significant investment in your health, our experts say you should always consult your doctor before purchasing an outdoor sauna or starting a sauna routine—especially if you have severe cardiovascular or lung issues.

The cost of an outdoor sauna depends on several factors, including capacity, heat source, extra features, integrated technology, and materials. We found saunas at around $1,599 and others at up to $9,799, depending on your budget and needs.

Yes, outdoor saunas typically come with features and accessories to help weatherproof them (like shingles) and keep them dry and ventilated during winter.

When investing in an outdoor sauna, you have to consider its costs, including the electricity used by electric heaters, lighting, and more. When purchasing an outdoor sauna, look for the wattage and amount of electricity it needs to run; it doesn’t hurt to crunch the numbers to estimate your electric bill with a sauna in the mix.

#8812. Texas A&M Study Shows Creatine Adding Muscle Mass Gains Without Lifting

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

For better brain cognition through to superior strength and power, creatine is one of those supplements that seems to actually work. Thanks to its cell volumizing and energizing abilities, creatine allows us to lift heavier, recover faster, and focus better under stress. Now, a new study from Texas A&M University is touting that creatine can construct more muscle even without a structured resistance training program.

The study, published in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, suggests that creatine could help adults to maintain lean tissue and strength, even without regular exercise. Of course, maintaining adequate levels of muscle mass is particularly important as we age because muscle loss, also known as sarcopenia, can begin as early as 35 years, and typically sees lean mass decline at a rate of 1 to 2 percent, per year, for the average person. In fact, those who fail to engage with regular resistance training could lose as much as 4 to 6 pounds of muscle per decade.

New meta-analyses show this tried and true supp can benefit both men and women—but you still have to...

For 12 weeks, men and women between the ages of 45 and 65 were provided with creatine or a maltodextrin placebo, with each group being split into those who wanted to participate in a supervised, structured exercise program, and those who didn’t want to commit to the organized sessions. As the participants filled out questionnaires during the study, data showed that the structured exercise group racked up more moderate-to-vigorous activity than those who weren’t locked in.

Despite lower levels of activity, those who took two 5g doses of creatine per day, and were not in the structured exercise program, increased their lean tissue by around 2.4 pounds over the 12-week study period. Conversely, those who took the placebo lost almost half a pound. “Creatine Monohydrate supplementation without exercise training and diet intervention increased lean tissue mass, strength, and muscular endurance while promoting favorable changes in selected blood lipids, HbA1c, and selected markers of cognitive function and memory,” read the report.

The results on muscle mass were even more profound in the structured exercise group, however. Creatine users who undertook the supervised sessions gained 2.8 pounds of lean mass on average. Creatine was also shown to preserve muscle even under the conditions of fat loss, because participants in the exercise program were given a modest calorie deficit. After 12 weeks, this group had gained almost three pounds of lean tissue despite dropping fat, while the exercise group that took a placebo showed little change in lean tissue. Still, both the structured and non-structured groups, on creatine, saw a greater reduction in body fat percentage than that seen by exercise or diet alone.

“Creatine Monohydrate supplementation with and without exercise and diet intervention may help middle-aged and older adults maintain muscle mass and strength while favorably affecting selected markers of health and cognitive function,” concluded the study.

#8811. Common Reasons Diets Stop Working After a While

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Early progress on a weight-loss plan can give way to a stretch where the same effort no longer produces the same results. That shift reflects a set of predictable physiological and behavioral forces that push back against restrictive eating.

Below are nine of those forces and how each one slows progress.

As body weight drops, the body burns fewer calories at rest, partly because it starts conserving energy.

Researchers call this adaptive thermogenesis. A 2026 randomized trial published in the Journal of Human Nutrition and Dietetics detected it within the first week of reduced energy intake. Over time, the same plan produces less progress, even when effort stays consistent.

Weight loss pushes appetite in the wrong direction.

As the body’s energy stores shrink, hunger increases and meals feel less filling. Steeper cuts in food intake intensify both signals, and that pressure makes aggressive restriction hard to sustain.

Banning a food intensifies the desire for it. Eliminating a food works against established habits and social life at the same time, so the plan ends and the banned foods return.

Restrictive weight loss draws energy from muscle as well as fat. Muscle burns energy even at rest, so losing it lowers metabolism further.

A 2025 paper from Reviews in Endocrine & Metabolic Disorders reports that regained weight disproportionately returns as fat rather than as the lean tissue that was lost. The method of weight loss influences how much muscle the body keeps.

In a peer-reviewed randomized controlled trial published in Obesity Science & Practice, participants on the Trilivy™ Reset 5 & 1 Plan retained 98% of lean mass and reduced visceral fat by 14% over 16 weeks.*

“A weight management program that protects lean mass, reduces visceral fat, and builds habit infrastructure is designed for the years after the active weight loss phase and addresses the conditions that drive regain at the source,” said Satya Jonnalagadda, PhD, MBA, RD, Vice President, Scientific & Clinical Affairs at Trilivy.

Constant restriction demands steady mental effort, and a single stressful event can be enough to derail a plan.

Coaching gives people support to continue their plan through stressful periods.

In the same trial from Obesity Science & Practice, participants with coach support lost up to 10 times more weight and 17 times more fat than those in a self-directed group. Trilivy coaches provide accountability and real-time support that help keep a plan on track.

“In a world of automation and AI, human connection is our superpower,” Jonnalagadda said. “A coach can meet a person in the exact moment a routine breaks down, and that is something a notification has never been able to do.”

A pass-fail approach to eating leaves no room for an imperfect meal. Under that framework, deviation from a meal plan feels like a reason to stop, and each restart interrupts the consistency that progress builds on.

Small, untracked additions, like a slightly larger serving or a few bites while cooking, add energy without registering as a meal. Weight loss also prompts the body to reduce spontaneous movement, which lowers daily energy use.

Both shifts happen gradually, and together they slow progress.

In a 2026 study from Annals of Internal Medicine, adults who slept about 80 minutes less per night gained roughly a pound and became more sedentary over six weeks. Their weight gain tracked closely with the drop in daily movement.

The finding connects short sleep to reduced activity, one of the everyday inputs a weight-loss plan relies on.

Restaurant meals, birthdays, work events, and holidays bring menus, timing and traditions that differ from an established meal plan.

Rules designed around a home kitchen do not offer guidance for those moments. A plan that accounts for eating out and celebrations gives people a way to navigate them.

Each of these nine factors traces back to two pressures: a body that works to protect its energy stores and daily routines that strict rules don’t account for.

A sustainable approach to weight management addresses both. It protects lean muscle, pairs balanced nutrition and physical activity with healthy daily habits, and builds in coaching and accountability that continue past the initial results, supporting long-term metabolic health.

Trilivy™ recommends that you contact your healthcare provider before starting and throughout your weight loss journey.

* Arterburn LM, et al. Randomized controlled trial assessing two commercial weight loss programs in adults with overweight or obesity. Obesity Science & Practice. 2019. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/osp4.312. In a clinical study, individuals on the Reset 5 & 1 Plan experienced a reduction of 14% visceral fat and 98% of lean mass was retained at 16 weeks. Those on the Reset 5 & 1 Plan with the support of a coach lost up to 10x more weight and 17x more fat than those who tried to lose weight on their own.

M&F and editorial staff were not involved in the creation of this content.
